articles.title: Endobronchial Valves for Persistent Air Leak and Bronchopleural Fistula in Children: A Systematic Review of Indications, Procedural Approaches, and Outcomes.
articles.dek: A systematic review of 13 reports found that endobronchial or intrabronchial valve placement may help selected children with persistent air leak or bronchopleural fistula when conservative care fails, though evidence remains limited.
summary: This systematic review searched PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar through June 2026 for pediatric and late-adolescent cases treated with bronchoscopic valve placement for persistent air leak (PAL), bronchopleural fistula (BPF), or pneumothorax with ongoing air leak. Thirteen reports—comprising case reports, case series, and observational studies—were included with extractable pediatric data; no language restrictions were applied.

Valve placement achieved rapid or eventual air-leak improvement in selected children across several contexts: necrotizing pneumonia, postoperative air leak, chronic ventilator dependence, malignancy, and ECMO support. Reported complications included valve migration or loosening, granulation tissue, minor hemoptysis, atelectasis, contralateral pneumothorax, and recurrent air leak; many children underwent uncomplicated valve removal.

The authors conclude that endobronchial or intrabronchial valves may serve as rescue or bridge therapy for carefully selected children with refractory PAL or BPF, but acknowledge that evidence certainty remains low due to small sample sizes, retrospective design, inconsistent outcome definitions, and possible publication bias. Prospective multicenter registries with standardized reporting are needed to clarify optimal patient selection, timing, and safety.
articles.why: Persistent air leak and bronchopleural fistula are serious complications in critically ill children, particularly those recovering from necrotizing pneumonia, surgery, or ECMO. Current management options are limited when conservative therapy and high-risk surgery are exhausted. This review documents the emerging use of a minimally invasive bronchoscopic approach and may inform clinical teams considering options for refractory cases, though it does not constitute evidence for routine adoption.
articles.evidence: Systematic review synthesizing 13 case reports, case series, and observational studies. Exact sample size across all studies not reported in abstract. Major limitations include small individual samples, predominantly retrospective design, variable definitions of success and adverse events across studies, and inherent publication bias toward positive outcomes. No randomized trials identified. Evidence certainty is low. Prospective data are lacking.

articles.title: Medication non-adherence and its associated factors among heart failure patients in Africa: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.dek: A systematic review of 17 African studies found that approximately 42% of heart failure patients do not take their medications as prescribed, with lack of health insurance, multiple medications, and other chronic conditions as key associated factors.
summary: This systematic review and meta-analysis synthesized observational studies published between 2000 and 2025 involving 6,276 heart failure patients across multiple African regions. The authors searched PubMed/MEDLINE, African Journal Online, and Google Scholar, and assessed study quality using Joanna Briggs Institute checklists. Data were pooled using random-effects modeling.

The pooled prevalence of medication non-adherence was 41.88% (95% CI: 25.43–58.34), with substantial regional variation—Western Africa showed the highest rate at 77.59%. Meta-analysis identified lack of health insurance as the strongest predictor of non-adherence (odds ratio 4.27), followed by polypharmacy (odds ratio 2.58) and presence of comorbidities (odds ratio 1.76).

The authors conclude that financial barriers, clinical complexity, and therapy-related challenges drive non-adherence across the continent and recommend expanding insurance coverage, implementing medication subsidies, simplifying medication regimens, and developing region-tailored adherence support strategies. The extreme heterogeneity across studies (I² = 99.7%) suggests findings vary considerably by setting and population.
articles.why: Heart failure outcomes depend critically on consistent medication use. This review documents non-adherence as a major obstacle in African health systems and identifies modifiable factors—particularly insurance access and medication burden—that may inform policy and clinical program design in resource-limited settings. Understanding regional variation is relevant for tailoring interventions to local health infrastructure and economic contexts.
articles.evidence: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 17 observational studies (cross-sectional and cohort) totaling 6,276 patients. No randomized trials were included. Major limitations include extreme heterogeneity across studies (I² = 99.7%), which the authors explored through subgroup analysis but which limits the precision of the overall prevalence estimate. The authors do not report whether all relevant African countries or health systems were represented, and adherence measurement methods across studies are not detailed in the abstract. No publication bias was detected by Egger's test (p = 0.267).

articles.title: Endpoint-specific mortality associated with malignancy among adults with sepsis or septic shock: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.dek: In adults with sepsis or septic shock, malignancy is associated with elevated mortality across multiple timeframes, with the strongest associations observed at intermediate and extended follow-up.
summary: This systematic review and meta-analysis examined 105 studies (20,089,138 participants total) to determine whether malignancy affects mortality risk in sepsis or septic shock. The researchers searched five medical databases through September 2025 and grouped mortality endpoints into five categories: ICU, in-hospital, early, intermediate, and extended follow-up mortality. Eighty-five studies contributing 101 endpoint estimates were included in the primary analysis.

Patients with sepsis and concurrent malignancy showed higher mortality across all endpoints examined. The strongest associations were observed at intermediate follow-up (odds ratio 2.28) and extended follow-up (odds ratio 2.41), while in-hospital and early mortality showed odds ratios of 1.90 and 1.81 respectively. ICU mortality showed a smaller association (odds ratio 1.21, with confidence interval crossing 1.0). Associations persisted in haematologic malignancies and were concentrated in in-hospital and early mortality for metastatic disease, while solid tumours showed more modest associations.

The authors note that reported estimates are unadjusted and therefore reflect overall prognostic associations rather than independent causal effects of malignancy. Sensitivity analyses using risk ratios generally produced smaller estimates than odds ratios. Heterogeneity across studies appeared partly attributable to severity-related variables, though substantial variation remained unexplained.
articles.why: These findings suggest that clinicians should recognize malignancy as a prognostic factor in sepsis outcomes and consider tailoring discussions of illness trajectory and mortality risk according to cancer type and disease stage. The endpoint-specific variation—particularly the stronger associations at later follow-up timepoints—may inform discussions about both acute intensive care goals and longer-term recovery expectations. However, because estimates are unadjusted, they do not establish a causal mechanism and should not be interpreted as capturing the independent effect of malignancy apart from other patient factors.
articles.evidence: Observational meta-analysis of 105 studies (85 contributing to primary synthesis) totalling 20,089,138 participants. Design: systematic review with random-effects meta-analysis and subgroup, meta-regression, and sensitivity analyses. Major limitations and uncertainty include: (1) all primary estimates were unadjusted for covariates, precluding causal inference; (2) substantial heterogeneity across endpoints and clinical contexts, only partially explained by exploratory meta-regression; (3) studies used varied definitions and timeframes for mortality endpoints; (4) risk ratio estimates were generally smaller than odds ratios, suggesting potential variation in effect measurement depending on outcome frequency; (5) the abstract does not specify the proportion of included studies reporting adjusted versus unadjusted estimates, nor does it characterize the quality or study designs of included reports.

articles.title: Safety and immunogenicity of the 24-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine in healthy Chinese adults: two single-center, randomized, double-blind Phase 1 and Phase 2 trials.
articles.dek: A 24-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine showed favorable safety and immunogenicity in Chinese adults aged 18 years and older across two randomized controlled trials.
summary: Two single-center, randomized, double-blind Phase 1 and Phase 2 trials enrolled 240 and 992 participants respectively. Phase 1 compared low-dose and high-dose PCV24, PPSV23 (23-valent pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine), and placebo. Phase 2 randomized participants to three PCV24 formulations (low-dose with low adjuvant, low-dose, and high-dose) or PPSV23. Participants were healthy Chinese adults aged 18 years or older.

Adverse reactions within 30 days post-vaccination were predominantly grade 1–2 severity, with rare grade 3 events occurring only in the 0–7 day window. No vaccine-related serious adverse events were reported over 6 months. In Phase 2 immunogenicity analysis, the PCV24 high-dose group met non-inferiority criteria for IgG seroconversion across all 24 serotypes when compared with PPSV23.

The findings suggest PCV24 demonstrates acceptable tolerability and generates robust immune responses against the 24 serotypes tested in this population. Authors concluded the safety profile and immunogenicity warrant further efficacy evaluation in larger populations, though clinical benefit in preventing pneumococcal disease remains to be established.
articles.why: Pneumococcal vaccination strategies have traditionally relied on vaccines covering fewer serotypes. A 24-valent vaccine could broaden serotype coverage and potentially reduce invasive pneumococcal disease risk. These early-phase data in Chinese adults provide foundational safety and immunogenicity information relevant to vaccine development pipelines and inform discussions about serotype breadth in conjugate vaccine design. Generalizability to other populations and long-term clinical outcomes remain to be determined.
articles.evidence: Randomized, double-blind, controlled trial design (Phase 1 and Phase 2). Phase 1 n=240; Phase 2 n=992. Limitations: single-center design limits generalizability; abstract does not specify blinding duration, exact seroconversion percentages, or comparator immunogenicity data; no efficacy data (prevention of pneumococcal disease); follow-up was 6 months for serious adverse events but timeframe for immunogenicity assessments is not stated; clinical relevance of non-inferiority for IgG seroconversion to disease prevention is uncertain without efficacy trials.

articles.title: Evaluating a multi-vaccine respiratory immunization strategy involving SARS-CoV-2, pneumococcal, and influenza vaccines in adults: A randomized, open-label, multicenter, controlled, non-inferiority Phase IV trial in China.
articles.dek: A randomized Phase IV trial in China found that co-administering inactivated SARS-CoV-2, pneumococcal, and influenza vaccines together preserved immune responses and maintained acceptable safety compared with separate administration.
summary: This randomized, open-label, multicenter Phase IV trial enrolled 1,404 adults aged ≥18 years in China (with equal representation of ages 18–59 and ≥60 years). Participants were assigned 1:1:1 to three groups: SARS-CoV-2 vaccine (WIBP-CorV) plus pneumococcal vaccine (PPV23) on Day 0 and WIBP-CorV plus influenza vaccine (IIV4) on Day 28; WIBP-CorV alone on Days 0 and 28; or PPV23 on Day 0 followed by IIV4 on Day 28. The study evaluated whether co-administration maintained immune responses (non-inferiority design) and safety.

Co-administration preserved humoral immune responses across all three vaccine platforms. Non-inferiority in geometric mean titers or concentrations was demonstrated for SARS-CoV-2 neutralizing antibodies and pneumococcal serotype-specific IgG responses. Seroconversion rates were non-inferior for all pneumococcal serotypes; however, results were described as 'less consistent' for SARS-CoV-2 after the second dose and influenza A(H1N1). Age-stratified findings were noted to require cautious interpretation.

The safety profile was acceptable, with only slightly elevated rates of mild, transient local reactions and no vaccine-related serious adverse events reported. These results support the feasibility of co-administering these three vaccines while maintaining immunogenicity and safety in the study population, potentially streamlining adult respiratory immunization programs.
articles.why: Combined respiratory pathogen vaccination may reduce clinical burden and improve immunization completion rates in adults. This trial provides empirical safety and immunogenicity data relevant to vaccine co-administration strategies, though applicability to other populations and vaccine formulations requires consideration. Results may inform discussion of vaccination schedules and program logistics.
articles.evidence: Randomized controlled trial (non-inferiority design), open-label, multicenter. Sample size: 1,404 adults. Major limitations: open-label design (no blinding); results for SARS-CoV-2 after second dose and influenza A(H1N1) seroconversion described as 'less consistent' without specification of numerical thresholds; age-stratified findings require cautious interpretation per authors; study conducted in China with specific vaccine formulation (WIBP-CorV) limiting generalizability; no numerical effect sizes, confidence intervals, or p-values provided in abstract; specific non-inferiority margins not stated in abstract.

articles.title: Comparison of the Safety and Efficacy of Remimazolam for Sedation in Adults Undergoing Fiberoptic Bronchoscopy: A Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
articles.dek: A meta-analysis of 16 randomized controlled trials found remimazolam, a novel ultra-short-acting benzodiazepine, reduced respiratory depression, hypotension, and bradycardia compared with other sedatives during fiberoptic bronchoscopy in adults.
summary: This meta-analysis systematically reviewed randomized controlled trials comparing remimazolam with dexmedetomidine, midazolam, and propofol for sedation during fiberoptic bronchoscopy in adults. The analysis included 16 trials enrolling 2,325 patients and evaluated safety outcomes (respiratory depression, hypotension, bradycardia), procedural outcomes (time to target sedation, success rate, emergence time), and postanesthesia recovery metrics.

Remimazolam demonstrated significantly lower rates of respiratory depression (relative risk 0.51), hypotension (relative risk 0.50), and bradycardia (relative risk 0.37) compared with control sedatives. Remimazolam onset was faster than dexmedetomidine by approximately 2.2 minutes but slightly slower than propofol. Procedure success rates were comparable across all sedatives. Remimazolam showed faster emergence and shorter postanesthesia care unit stays compared with both dexmedetomidine and midazolam.

The findings suggest remimazolam may offer a favorable safety profile for bronchoscopy sedation, particularly regarding respiratory and hemodynamic stability, with rapid recovery characteristics. However, the clinical significance of these differences and applicability across varied clinical settings require consideration of individual patient factors and institutional protocols.
articles.why: These results are relevant to clinicians and proceduralists considering sedation options for fiberoptic bronchoscopy, where maintaining airway reflexes and hemodynamic stability while ensuring adequate sedation remains clinically important. The comparative safety profile—particularly regarding respiratory depression and hemodynamic effects—may inform sedation selection discussions, though effectiveness appears similar across agents. Faster emergence and recovery times could influence resource planning and patient throughput considerations.
articles.evidence: Design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials through January 2026. Sample: 16 RCTs with 2,325 patients total. Major limitations and uncertainties: The abstract does not specify heterogeneity measures (I² values), publication bias assessment methods, or quality scoring of included trials. Comparative efficacy relied on trials with different control agents rather than a single head-to-head comparison. Specific inclusion/exclusion criteria for trials, patient characteristics (age, comorbidity burden), dosing regimens, and whether analyses were intention-to-treat are not detailed. The clinical meaningfulness of differences in emergence and PACU stay times (minutes range) is unclear. Long-term safety outcomes are not addressed.

articles.title: Berberine improves diabetic foot ulcer healing after tibial transverse osteotomy by inhibiting the PDGF-B/PDGFRβ signaling pathway.
articles.dek: In a randomized trial, berberine injections added to tibial transverse osteotomy improved diabetic foot ulcer healing rates and reduced inflammatory markers in patients with Wagner grade 2–4 ulcers.
summary: This prospective, randomized, placebo-controlled trial enrolled 96 diabetic foot ulcer patients (Wagner grade 2–4) scheduled for tibial transverse osteotomy (TTO), randomized 1:1 to receive either TTO plus local berberine injections (n=48) or TTO plus saline placebo (n=48). All participants completed 3-month follow-up with no dropouts. An additional 10 diabetic and 10 healthy controls were included for exploratory cellular studies only.

The berberine group demonstrated a higher total effective rate of ulcer healing at 3 months (87.5% vs. 68.8%; risk difference 18.7%; P < 0.05) and greater improvements in ankle-brachial index (ABI), ulcer healing rate, and inflammatory markers (hs-CRP and IL-6) compared to surgery alone. Berberine was associated with reduced fibroblast apoptosis in wound tissue and lower protein expression of PDGF-B and PDGFRβ. No severe adverse events were reported.

The authors propose that berberine's benefits may involve downregulation of the PDGF-B/PDGFRβ signaling pathway and reduced inflammation. However, the findings are correlative, and the mechanistic role of PDGF-B/PDGFRβ pathway inhibition remains unvalidated. Larger multi-center trials are needed to confirm efficacy and establish safety in broader populations.
articles.why: Diabetic foot ulcers remain a major cause of morbidity and lower-limb complications. This trial suggests adjunctive berberine—a natural compound with anti-inflammatory properties—may enhance surgical healing outcomes in a defined subgroup. If confirmed, such an approach might inform discussions about adjunctive therapies for patients undergoing TTO; however, the findings are preliminary and based on a single-center trial with a modest sample size. The correlation between PDGF pathway markers and clinical benefit requires mechanistic clarification before pathway-specific claims can be made.

evidence.design: Prospective, single-center, randomized, placebo-controlled, parallel-group, blinded trial.
evidence.sample_size: 96 randomized participants (48 berberine, 48 placebo); 10 diabetic and 10 healthy controls for exploratory studies only.
evidence.primary_outcome: Total effective rate of ulcer healing at 3 months.
evidence.secondary_outcomes: Changes in ABI, ulcer area, VAS pain score, and serum inflammatory markers (hs-CRP, IL-6).
evidence.exploratory_outcomes: Serum VEGF, bFGF, PDGF-B levels and fibroblast apoptosis in wound tissue.
major_limitations: Modest sample size (96 randomized) provides relatively narrow confidence intervals around primary outcome.
Trial registration number not reported in abstract.
Publication date and peer-review status not confirmed from abstract alone.
Mechanistic findings (PDGF-B/PDGFRβ pathway) are correlative; causality is not established.
No information on blinding methodology or allocation concealment detail.
Longer-term follow-up duration not reported; 3-month endpoint may not capture late complications or durability.
evidence.uncertainty: The PDGF-B/PDGFRβ pathway reduction observed may be a marker of improved healing rather than a mechanistic driver. Further studies are needed to establish whether berberine's effect is direct, indirect, or context-dependent. Safety and efficacy in other patient populations and surgical contexts remain unknown.

articles.title: Gut virome remodeling after fecal microbiota transplantation is associated with virus-bacteria co-variation and metabolic response in obesity and type 2 diabetes.
articles.dek: Viral community changes in the gut after fecal microbiota transplantation show patterns associated with metabolic response in obesity and type 2 diabetes, comparable to bacterial changes.
summary: This randomized controlled trial analyzed viral and bacterial populations in longitudinal stool samples from patients with obesity and type 2 diabetes who received fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) alone, FMT combined with lifestyle intervention, or sham treatment with lifestyle intervention. Researchers used specialized sequencing to examine virus-like particles and bacterial DNA alongside clinical metabolic markers including LDL cholesterol response.

Post-FMT viral community changes distinguished LDL responders from non-responders with 84.8% accuracy, comparable to bacterial classification accuracy (81.4%). Donor-derived viral sequences were detected in 64.7% of FMT-alone recipients and 58.8% of FMT plus lifestyle intervention recipients, compared to 5.6% in the sham-plus-lifestyle group. The virome became more diverse after FMT, shifted toward donor composition, and showed coordinated associations with specific bacterial species.

Most responsive viruses belonged to the Caudoviricetes class and were predicted to infect common gut bacteria including Roseburia, Bifidobacterium, Escherichia, Blautia, and Enterococcus. The authors propose that viral community structure represents an ecological component contributing to clinical response heterogeneity in FMT, beyond bacterial changes alone.
articles.why: Clinical FMT responses vary substantially between patients. These findings suggest viral-bacterial interactions may partially explain this heterogeneity and could inform future monitoring strategies. Understanding whether virome composition predicts metabolic outcomes might eventually help identify which patients are likely to benefit from FMT, though current evidence does not support modifying clinical practice.

evidence.design: Randomized controlled trial with longitudinal sampling
evidence.sample_size: 52 total subjects (17 FMT alone, 17 FMT with lifestyle intervention, 18 sham with lifestyle intervention); viral engraftment assessed in subgroup of 17 per arm
evidence.major_limitations: Abstract does not report statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or effect sizes for metabolic or clinical outcomes. Precise timing of sample collection relative to FMT is not specified. Predictive associations between viral contigs and bacterial hosts are computational predictions, not validated experimentally. Long-term durability of virome changes unknown from this report. Full results and detailed methods unavailable from abstract alone.

articles.title: From Bench to Bedside: Evaluating the Accuracy of Clinical Sensory Testing in Detecting Somatosensory Disorders. A Systematic Review.
articles.dek: Clinical sensory tests show moderate-to-high specificity but variable sensitivity for detecting somatosensory disorders, with composite tools performing better than single modalities.
summary: This systematic review identified 12 studies (N=4,911 participants) evaluating Clinical Sensory Testing (CST) accuracy across populations with various somatosensory conditions including diabetic peripheral neuropathy, lumbar spinal stenosis, and neuropathic pain. Studies compared CST results against reference standards and were assessed for methodological quality using QUADAS-2.

Results were organized by sensory modality. The Semmes-Weinstein Monofilament Test (pressure/touch) showed 77%–90.7% sensitivity and 63.8%–100% specificity. Tuning fork vibration tests ranged from 30%–96% sensitivity and 45%–99% specificity. Thermal tests exhibited the greatest variability (0.0%–97.1% sensitivity; 2.0%–94.4% specificity). Composite tools combining multiple modalities demonstrated the highest accuracy, often exceeding 87% for both measures.

The authors conclude that CSTs are pragmatic for preliminary sensory profiling, particularly in multimodal combinations, but substantial variability and methodological limitations preclude reliable stand-alone diagnostic use. The review identified high or unclear risk of bias in most included studies and calls for protocol standardization and validation against robust reference standards before routine clinical integration.
articles.why: Clinicians use bedside sensory tests to detect peripheral and central somatosensory dysfunction. This review clarifies that individual tests have inconsistent accuracy and may miss cases or incorrectly identify dysfunction when used in isolation. The finding that composite approaches perform better may support the clinical practice of combining multiple sensory modalities rather than relying on single tests, though further standardized validation is needed before changing diagnostic algorithms.

evidence.design: Systematic review and narrative synthesis of comparative accuracy studies
evidence.major_limitations: High or unclear risk of bias in most included studies; wide methodological heterogeneity across studies; substantial variation in sensitivity and specificity intervals, particularly for thermal testing; no pooled meta-analysis reported; full-text access and specific details of bias domains not available from abstract
evidence.uncertainty: The abstract does not specify whether trials were registered, provide confidence intervals around reported ranges, or detail reasons for high RoB ratings. Causes of sensitivity/specificity variability (e.g., differences in reference standards, population characteristics, test protocols) are not explained in the abstract.
